Multiple Regression: More than One Predictor

Dormann (2020), Environmental Data Analysis — Chapters 15 and 16

Emiel van Loon

today

Where we are going

Every model so far had one predictor. Adding a second one is, in principle, just one more row in the coefficient table — but four things get complicated. At the end of this chapter you should…

  • be able to visualise data and models with two predictors (panels, symbols, image/contour plots)
  • know what a statistical interaction is, how it is coded, how you recognise it in a figure and in the output, and how to read the equations from a coefficient table
  • recognise collinearity between predictors, know what it does to a model (VIF) and what to do about it
  • understand model selection: the marginality principle, AIC vs BIC vs likelihood-ratio test, backward stepwise selection and best-subset regression — and their pitfalls

Skipped from Dormann: principal component analysis (15.3.1, 16.2.1), the two-way ANOVA by hand (15.4.1) and the matrix algebra (15.5). Practical 5 is a reading practical: you interpret output, you do not write code.

One more predictor: what changes?

ft_add <- glm(surv ~ age + sex, family = binomial, data = tit)
knitr::kable(coef(summary(ft_add)), digits = c(4, 4, 2, 6))
Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) 1.2354 0.1920 6.43 0.000000
age -0.0043 0.0052 -0.82 0.413925
sexmale -2.4607 0.1523 -16.16 0.000000

Survival of 1046 Titanic passengers, survived ~ age + sex. Each predictor gets its own maximum-likelihood estimate; a 42-year-old man survives with probability \(\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(1.235 - 0.00425 \cdot 42 - 2.46) = 0.20\). Nothing new — except that four complications now arise:

  1. Visualising — a figure has only two axes
  2. Interactions — the effect of one predictor may depend on the other
  3. Collinearity — predictors that carry the same information
  4. Model selection — which of the many candidate models to report

“Multiple” regression = several predictors, one response. (Multivariate statistics means several responses — a different topic.)

1. Visualising two categorical predictors

parset(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.4, 0.8), cex.main = 1.2)
for (sp in c("C", "S")) {
  d <- subset(cormorant, subspecies == sp)
  stripchart(divetime ~ season, data = d, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
             jitter = 0.08, pch = 19, col = pal["dark"], ylim = c(8, 30),
             ylab = "dive time [min]", xlab = "season",
             main = paste("subspecies", sp))
}
stripchart(divetime ~ season, data = subset(cormorant, subspecies == "C"),
           vertical = TRUE, at = 1:4 - 0.12, pch = 19, col = pal["accent"],
           ylim = c(8, 30), ylab = "dive time [min]", xlab = "season",
           main = "all in one", xlim = c(0.5, 4.5))
stripchart(divetime ~ season, data = subset(cormorant, subspecies == "S"),
           vertical = TRUE, at = 1:4 + 0.12, pch = 1, col = pal["accent2"], add = TRUE)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", pch = c(19, 1), col = pal[c("accent", "accent2")],
       legend = c("carbo", "sinensis"))

Dive times of two European cormorant subspecies, P. carbo carbo (C) and P. c. sinensis (S), in four seasons (Dormann Figs 15.1, 15.2). Panel plots (left, middle) give a quick overview; an all-in-one plot (right) needs more work but takes less space. Either way we see the same thing: dive time increases over the year in both subspecies, and the smaller sinensis dives a little shorter. A continuous x works the same way — one panel, or one symbol, per level of the factor.

Visualising binary data: smooth first

parset(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(surv ~ age, data = tit, pch = "|", col = adjustcolor(pal["dark"], 0.3),
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "survived", xlab = "age", main = "raw 0/1 data")
axis(2, at = 0:1, labels = c("no", "yes"))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 80), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "age", ylab = "survival",
     main = "moving average (LOESS)")
for (s in c("female", "male")) {
  d <- subset(tit, sex == s)
  for (sp in c(0.2, 0.5, 0.75)) {
    lo <- loess(surv ~ age, data = d, span = sp)
    xs <- seq(min(d$age), max(d$age), length = 100)
    lines(xs, predict(lo, data.frame(age = xs)), lwd = 2,
          lty = ifelse(s == "female", 1, 2),
          col = adjustcolor(ifelse(s == "female", pal["accent2"], pal["accent"]),
                            c(1, 0.6, 0.35)[match(sp, c(0.2, 0.5, 0.75))]))
  }
  rug(d$age, side = ifelse(s == "female", 3, 1), col = ifelse(s == "female", pal["accent2"], pal["accent"]))
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = 1:2, col = pal[c("accent2", "accent")],
       legend = c("female", "male"))

Titanic survival against age (Dormann Figs 15.3–15.5). A panel or scatter plot of 0/1 data shows nothing (left). A moving average (LOESS: a local regression in a sliding window, span 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.75 from dark to light) makes the pattern visible: women survived at a high rate at every age, men’s survival dropped steeply with age. The window width is a choice — narrow traces the data, wide smooths it. Note the two curves are not parallel: that is an interaction.

2. Interactions: when one effect depends on the other

parset(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.4, 0.8), cex.main = 1.2)
x <- 1:2
draw <- function(a, b, main) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0.7, 2.3), ylim = c(0, 10), xaxt = "n", xlab = "predictor 1",
       ylab = "response", main = main)
  axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("low", "high"))
  lines(x, a, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["dark"])
  lines(x, b, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["accent2"])
}
draw(c(2, 6), c(4, 8), "no interaction: parallel")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = pal[c("dark", "accent2")],
       legend = c("predictor 2 = A", "predictor 2 = B"))
draw(c(2, 6), c(2, 9), "synergistic")
draw(c(2, 8), c(5, 3), "antagonistic")

What does a plant need to grow? Water and light. More light helps — but only if there is enough water. That is a statistical interaction: the effect of one predictor depends on the value of the other (Dormann Fig. 15.6). In a figure you recognise it as lines with different slopes; parallel lines mean purely additive effects. Tropical trees grow because heat and rain come in the right combination; on the Titanic the effect of age depends on sex.

How an interaction enters the model: multiply

passenger sex age sex × age
Miss Allen female (0) 29.0 0
Master Allison male (1) 0.9 0.9
Mrs Allison female (0) 25.0 0
Mr Anderson male (1) 48.0 48.0

The factor is a dummy (0/1). Multiplying it with age gives a new variable that is zero for all women — an effect of age that applies to men only. R does this for you: age * sex means age + sex + age:sex.

ft_int <- glm(surv ~ age * sex, family = binomial, data = tit)
knitr::kable(coef(summary(ft_int)), digits = c(4, 4, 2, 6))
Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) 0.4934 0.2542 1.94 0.052257
age 0.0225 0.0085 2.64 0.008342
sexmale -1.1541 0.3393 -3.40 0.000671
age:sexmale -0.0463 0.0112 -4.13 0.000037
  • age = the slope of age for women (the reference level): +0.023 per year
  • sexmale = the difference men − women at age 0
  • age:sexmale = how much steeper the age slope is for men: −0.046, so men: 0.023 − 0.046 = −0.024 per year

42-year-old man: \(\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(0.49 + 0.0225\cdot42 - 1.15 - 0.046\cdot42) = 0.11\); 42-year-old woman: the last two terms are × 0 → 0.73.

Two continuous predictors: the product is taken directly; positive = synergistic, negative = antagonistic (standardise first, or the larger one dominates). Beware: an unmodelled quadratic effect can masquerade as a significant interaction — test polynomials as well (Dormann footnote 4).

Reading the ANOVA table: sequential, and the marginality principle

a <- anova(ft_int, test = "Chisq")
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(a), digits = c(0, 1, 0, 1, 6))
Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev Pr(>Chi)
NULL NA NA 1045 1414.6 NA
age 1 3.2 1044 1411.4 0.071959
sex 1 310.0 1043 1101.3 0.000000
age:sex 1 17.9 1042 1083.4 0.000023

anova(fm) adds the terms one after the other (“sequentially”): each row tests what a term adds on top of the rows above it. Age alone explains almost nothing (P = 0.41); sex explains a lot; the interaction explains 17.9 more units — highly significant.

Do not conclude “age does not matter”. The significant interaction says that the main effects alone do not describe the pattern: the sexes differ strongly, but not among young children. Once an interaction is in the model, its main effects must stay — even if not significant — because the interaction contains them (Nelder’s marginality principle). And do not rank importance by the deviance column: with correlated predictors the order of the terms changes the numbers (but never the residual deviance).

Two categorical predictors: cormorants, additive vs interaction

fc_add <- glm(divetime ~ season + subspecies, family = gaussian, data = cormorant)
fc_int <- glm(divetime ~ season * subspecies, family = gaussian, data = cormorant)
ca <- coef(summary(fc_add))[, 1:2]
a  <- as.data.frame(anova(fc_int, test = "F"))[-1, c(1, 2, 5, 6)]
knitr::kable(ca, digits = 2)
Estimate Std. Error
(Intercept) 13.49 0.58
seasonsummer 3.23 0.74
seasonautumn 7.37 0.74
seasonwinter 11.59 0.74
subspeciesS -3.26 0.52 
knitr::kable(a, digits = c(0, 1, 1, 3))
Df Deviance F Pr(>F)
season 3 759.8 95.3 0.000
subspecies 1 106.0 39.9 0.000
season:subspecies 3 10.6 1.3 0.284 
parset()
m <- tapply(cormorant$divetime, list(cormorant$season, cormorant$subspecies), mean)
plot(1:4, m[, "C"], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["accent"], xaxt = "n",
     ylim = c(9, 28), xlab = "season", ylab = "mean dive time [min]", xlim = c(0.8, 4.2))
lines(1:4, m[, "S"], type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["accent2"])
pa <- predict(fc_add, newdata = expand.grid(season = levels(cormorant$season), subspecies = c("C", "S")))
lines(1:4, pa[1:4], lty = 2, col = pal["accent"]); lines(1:4, pa[5:8], lty = 2, col = pal["accent2"])
axis(1, at = 1:4, labels = levels(cormorant$season))
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = c(3, 3, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 2),
       col = c(pal["accent"], pal["accent2"], "grey40"),
       legend = c("carbo (cell means)", "sinensis (cell means)", "additive model"), cex = 0.9)

Left: coefficients of the additive model and anova(divetime ~ season * subspecies). The intercept is the reference cell (spring, C: 13.5 min); the season coefficients are differences from spring, subspeciesS the difference S − C (−3.3 min). A fitted value is a sum of coefficients: sinensis in autumn = 13.5 + 7.4 − 3.3 = 17.6 (or predict()). The interaction (3 df) is not significant (F = 1.4, P = 0.27): near-parallel lines, so we report the additive model. \(R^2\) = 90%: season 79%, subspecies 11% (partial \(R^2\) from the deviance column).

Continuous + categorical: the four models of an ANCOVA

parset(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4.2, 3.8, 2.4, 0.6), cex.main = 1.15)
tet$lconc <- log10(tet$conc)
pchs <- c(No = 1, Yes = 17)
base <- function(main) {
  plot(diameter ~ lconc, data = tet, pch = pchs[as.character(glucose)],
       col = pal["dark"], xlab = "log10(concentration)", ylab = "cell diameter", main = main)
}
base("a: intercept only"); abline(h = mean(tet$diameter), lwd = 2, col = pal["accent2"])
base("b: + concentration"); abline(lm(diameter ~ lconc, tet), lwd = 2, col = pal["accent2"])
base("c: + glucose"); cg <- coef(lm(diameter ~ glucose, tet))
abline(h = cg[1], lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = pal["accent2"]); abline(h = sum(cg), lwd = 2, col = pal["accent2"])
base("d: additive"); ca <- coef(lm(diameter ~ lconc + glucose, tet))
abline(ca[1], ca[2], lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = pal["accent2"]); abline(ca[1] + ca[3], ca[2], lwd = 2, col = pal["accent2"])
legend("topright", bty = "n", pch = c(1, 17), lty = c(2, 1), legend = c("without glucose", "with glucose"), cex = 0.85)

Diameter of Tetrahymena cells against culture density, with and without added glucose (Dormann Fig. 16.4; data after Dalgaard 2002). A model with a continuous and a categorical predictor is traditionally called ANCOVA — “analysis of covariance” — only for nostalgic reasons: it is just a GLM. (a) one mean; (b) one regression line; (c) two means; (d) the additive model diameter ~ log10(conc) + glucose: two parallel lines — the factor shifts the intercept, the slope is shared.

The fifth model: one slope per group

ft <- lm(diameter ~ lconc * glucose, data = tet)
parset()
plot(diameter ~ lconc, data = tet, pch = pchs[as.character(glucose)], col = pal["dark"],
     xlab = "log10(concentration)", ylab = "cell diameter")
for (gl in c("No", "Yes")) {
  d <- subset(tet, glucose == gl)
  xs <- seq(min(d$lconc), max(d$lconc), length = 50)
  pr <- predict(ft, newdata = data.frame(lconc = xs, glucose = gl), interval = "confidence")
  matlines(xs, pr, lty = c(1, 2, 2), lwd = c(3, 1, 1),
           col = ifelse(gl == "Yes", pal["accent"], pal["accent2"]))
}
legend("topright", bty = "n", pch = c(1, 17), lwd = 3, col = pal[c("accent2", "accent")],
       legend = c("without glucose", "with glucose"), cex = 0.9)

knitr::kable(coef(summary(ft)), digits = c(3, 3, 2, 4))
Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 37.559 0.988 38.03 0.0000
lconc -2.861 0.202 -14.19 0.0000
glucoseYes -1.122 1.219 -0.92 0.3618
lconc:glucoseYes 0.662 0.248 2.67 0.0104

Read the two lines straight from the table:

  • without glucose (reference): \(\hat y = 37.6 - 2.86 \cdot \log_{10}(\mathrm{conc})\)
  • with glucose: intercept and slope get their extra term: \(\hat y = (37.6 - 1.1) + (-2.86 + 0.66) \cdot \log_{10}(\mathrm{conc})\)

The interaction is significant (P = 0.01): the slopes differ. The glucose main effect (P = 0.36) is the intercept difference at log10(conc) = 0 — far outside the data, and it must stay in the model anyway.

Dormann Figs 16.3 / 16.5: lines only over the data range, 95% bands via predict(..., interval = "confidence") and matlines(). “Glucose does have an effect, but it is only detectable if we take the cell concentration into account.”

Two continuous predictors: C3 grasses in North America

panel.cor <- function(x, y, ...) {
  usr <- par("usr"); on.exit(par(usr)); par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
  r <- cor(x, y)
  text(0.5, 0.5, sprintf("%.2f", r), cex = 1 + 2 * abs(r),
       col = ifelse(abs(r) > 0.7, pal["accent2"], pal["dark"]))
}
pairs(paruelo[, c("MAP", "MAT", "JJAMAP", "DJFMAP")], pch = 19,
      col = adjustcolor(pal["dark"], 0.6), upper.panel = panel.cor, gap = 0.3)
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
## Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter

Proportion of C3 grasses (√-transformed) at 73 sites (Paruelo & Lauenroth 1996) against mean annual precipitation (MAP), temperature (MAT) and the fraction of summer (JJAMAP) and winter rain (DJFMAP).

Step 0: check the predictors. Summer and winter rain are strongly negatively correlated (r = −0.79 > 0.7): keep only one — JJAMAP, because growth happens in summer.

Step 1: the full model sqC3 ~ MAP * MAT * JJAMAP — 3 main effects, 3 two-way and 1 three-way interaction.

fp_full  <- lm(sqC3 ~ MAP * MAT * JJAMAP, data = paruelo)
fp_final <- lm(sqC3 ~ MAP + MAT * JJAMAP, data = paruelo)
a <- anova(fp_full)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(a)[-8, c(1, 2, 4, 5)], digits = c(0, 3, 2, 4))
Df Sum Sq F value Pr(>F)
MAP 1 0.000 0.00 0.9859
MAT 1 1.962 35.78 0.0000
JJAMAP 1 0.100 1.83 0.1808
MAP:MAT 1 0.030 0.54 0.4647
MAP:JJAMAP 1 0.016 0.29 0.5928
MAT:JJAMAP 1 0.282 5.14 0.0267
MAP:MAT:JJAMAP 1 0.000 0.00 0.9554

Only MAT:JJAMAP is significant, so the reduced model keeps MAP + MAT * JJAMAP (\(R^2_{adj}\) = 0.36 — “not too shabby for ecological data”). JJAMAP and MAT are not significant on their own but are part of the interaction, so they stay. Only MAP can be interpreted directly: more rain, more C3 grasses.

Visualising an interaction of two continuous predictors

parset(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.4, 1))
temperature <- seq(min(paruelo$MAT), max(paruelo$MAT), length = 50)
summerrain  <- seq(min(paruelo$JJAMAP), max(paruelo$JJAMAP), length = 50)
z <- outer(temperature, summerrain, function(X, Y)
  predict(fp_final, newdata = data.frame(MAP = mean(paruelo$MAP), MAT = X, JJAMAP = Y)))
image(temperature, summerrain, z, col = hcl.colors(50, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE),
      xlab = "mean annual temperature [°C]", ylab = "proportion of summer rain",
      main = "image + contour + data")
contour(temperature, summerrain, z, add = TRUE, labcex = 0.9)
points(paruelo$MAT, paruelo$JJAMAP, pch = 3)
ch <- chull(cbind(paruelo$MAT, paruelo$JJAMAP))
polygon(cbind(paruelo$MAT, paruelo$JJAMAP)[ch, ], lwd = 2)
plot(sqC3 ~ MAT, data = paruelo, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(pal["dark"], 0.5),
     xlab = "mean annual temperature [°C]", ylab = "sqrt(proportion C3)",
     main = "slices at three values of summer rain")
jj <- c(0.15, 0.30, 0.45); cols <- c(pal["accent3"], pal["accent"], pal["accent2"])
for (i in 1:3)
  lines(temperature, predict(fp_final, newdata = data.frame(MAP = mean(paruelo$MAP),
        MAT = temperature, JJAMAP = jj[i])), lwd = 3, col = cols[i])
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = cols, legend = paste("summer rain =", jj), cex = 0.9)

Dormann Figs 16.7–16.9. Two predictors plus a response need a surface: outer() evaluates predict() on a grid, image() colours it, contour() labels it — here at the mean MAP. The effect of temperature is steepest where summer rain is high: a continuous change of slope, the interaction. Always add the data points and their convex hull: the empty corners (hot and summer-wet) contain no observations, and predictions there have no basis. With every extra dimension this “curse of dimensionality” gets worse. Slices (right) are the poor man’s effect plot.

3. Collinearity: two predictors that say the same thing

parset()
plot(lElev ~ lArea, data = g, pch = 19, col = pal["dark"], xlab = "log(area)", ylab = "log(elevation)",
     main = sprintf("Galapagos: r = %.2f", cor(g$lArea, g$lElev)))
abline(lm(lElev ~ lArea, g), lwd = 2, col = pal["accent2"])

m_area <- glm.nb(Species ~ lArea, data = g)
m_elev <- glm.nb(Species ~ lElev, data = g)
m_both <- glm.nb(Species ~ lArea + lElev, data = g)
tab <- rbind(
  `Species ~ lArea`         = c(coef(summary(m_area))["lArea", 1:2], NA, NA),
  `Species ~ lElev`         = c(NA, NA, coef(summary(m_elev))["lElev", 1:2]),
  `Species ~ lArea + lElev` = c(coef(summary(m_both))["lArea", 1:2], coef(summary(m_both))["lElev", 1:2]))
colnames(tab) <- c("lArea", "SE", "lElev", "SE ")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3, format.args = list(nsmall = 3)) |> gsub(pattern = "NA", replacement = "")
lArea SE lElev SE
Species ~ lArea 0.367 0.036
Species ~ lElev 0.761 0.127
Species ~ lArea + lElev 0.389 0.065 -0.065 0.165

VIF of the two-predictor model: 3.3 — the variance of each coefficient is 3.3 × what it would be with uncorrelated predictors (SE of lArea: 0.036 → 0.065).

Bigger islands are higher. Alone, each predictor is “highly significant”; put both in and elevation drops to zero with a doubled standard error. Two problems (Dormann 15.3): we cannot attribute the effect to one of them (interpretation), and the likelihood surface becomes a flat ridge, so estimates are unstable and their errors inflated (estimation).

Diagnose before modelling: cor() / pairs() — |r| < 0.7 is safe. After modelling: car::vif() — values above 10 (Appalachian soils: 65,655!) mean a predictor has to go. The remedy in this course: keep one representative of each correlated group (Dormann’s PCA and cluster analysis are the alternatives).

4. Model selection: how many models, and which one?

The full model contains every predictor you consider reasonable, with interactions (and polynomials). Rule of thumb: 5–10 data points per model term (Harrell) — 100 observations allow ~10 terms; for 0/1 data count the rarer outcome.

With 14 terms there are \(2^{14}\) = 16 384 sub-models. Three strategies:

  • backward stepwise: start full, drop the term whose removal improves the criterion most, repeat (step())
  • forward stepwise: start empty, add — strongly discouraged: a predictor that only matters in an interaction never gets in
  • best subset: fit all sub-models and rank them (MuMIn::dredge())
parset()
k <- 1:12
train <- 1 - 0.85 * (1 - exp(-0.45 * k))
test  <- train + 0.02 * k^1.5 - 0.02
plot(k, train, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["accent"], ylim = c(0, 1.1),
     xlab = "number of terms in the model", ylab = "prediction error")
lines(k, test, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = pal["accent2"])
abline(v = k[which.min(test)], lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 3, col = pal[c("accent", "accent2")],
       legend = c("on the data used for fitting", "on new, independent data"))

Why not always keep the full model? It fits these data best and its estimates are unbiased — but it traces the data set. The variance–bias trade-off (schematic): with more terms the fit to the training data always improves, the error on new data first drops and then rises. Information criteria — AIC, BIC — balance fit (log-likelihood) against complexity (number of parameters) to find that minimum; BIC penalises harder and prefers smaller models. And every stepwise removal is a test, so selection distorts the p-values that survive.

Comparing two candidate models: AIC, BIC and the LR test

lrt <- anova(ft_add, ft_int, test = "Chisq")
tab <- data.frame(
  model = c("1: survived ~ age + sex", "2: survived ~ age * sex"),
  df = c(3, 4), `log-likelihood` = c(logLik(ft_add), logLik(ft_int)),
  AIC = AIC(ft_add, ft_int)$AIC, BIC = BIC(ft_add, ft_int)$BIC,
  `LR test: deviance` = c(NA, lrt$Deviance[2]), `P (chi-sq)` = c(NA, lrt$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 7))
model df log-likelihood AIC BIC LR test: deviance P (chi-sq)
1: survived ~ age + sex 3 -550.7 1107.3 1122.2 NA NA
2: survived ~ age * sex 4 -541.7 1091.4 1111.2 17.9 2.32e-05

Dormann’s Table 15.1: two ways to compare the additive and the interaction model of Titanic survival.

  • AIC / BIC: lower is better; a difference of ≥ 2 units is substantial (they live on the log-likelihood scale: 3.6 units ≈ 37-fold likelihood). Model 2 wins by 16 (AIC) and 11 (BIC) units.
  • Likelihood-ratio test (anova(m1, m2, test = "Chisq")): only for nested models; the deviance difference is \(\chi^2\) with df = difference in parameters. Here 17.9 on 1 df, P < 0.0001.
  • For quasi-models there is no likelihood, hence no AIC: use test = "F".

The criteria do not always agree — on the Titanic test data the simpler model even had the better \(R^2\). Which criterion, you decide beforehand; AIC (or BIC) is currently the standard.

Backward stepwise selection with step(): reading the output

ft_full <- glm(surv ~ sex * age * passengerClass, family = binomial, data = tit)
out <- capture.output(sB <- step(ft_full, k = log(nrow(tit)), steps = 1))
cat("```\n", paste(out[1:6], collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n", sep = "")
Start:  AIC=999.41
surv ~ sex * age * passengerClass

                         Df Deviance    AIC
- sex:age:passengerClass  2   917.84 987.37
<none>                        915.98 999.41
sBIC <- step(ft_full, k = log(nrow(tit)), trace = 0)
sAIC <- step(ft_full, trace = 0)

The full Titanic model sex * age * passengerClass (8 terms), first step of a BIC selection (k = log(n)). At every step step() tries to remove each removable term — only the three-way interaction here, because every other term is part of it (marginality!) — and lists the candidates by the criterion. <none> is the current model; anything above <none> improves the model when dropped, so the top term goes and the procedure repeats until <none> is on top.

tab <- data.frame(criterion = c("full model", "backward by AIC", "backward by BIC"),
                  `final model` = c(deparse(formula(ft_full)[[3]]),
                                    paste(deparse(formula(sAIC)[[3]]), collapse = ""),
                                    paste(deparse(formula(sBIC)[[3]]), collapse = "")),
                  terms = c(8, length(attr(terms(sAIC), "term.labels")), length(attr(terms(sBIC), "term.labels"))),
                  AIC = AIC(ft_full, sAIC, sBIC)$AIC, BIC = BIC(ft_full, sAIC, sBIC)$BIC, check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1))
criterion final model terms AIC BIC
full model sex * age * passengerClass 8 940.0 999.4
backward by AIC sex + age + passengerClass + sex:age + sex:passengerClass + age:passengerClass 6 937.8 987.4
backward by BIC sex + age + passengerClass + sex:passengerClass 4 946.0 980.7

AIC keeps all two-way interactions; BIC ends with sex:passengerClass only. Dormann’s warning: stepwise selection looks one step ahead — a removal that only pays off together with a second one is never found, so an AIC-driven step() can stop at a model with a worse AIC than a BIC-selected one. Not a panacea (Austin & Tu 2004); it gets more reliable with more data per term.

Best-subset regression: fit them all, then weigh

m_all <- glm.nb(Species ~ lArea + lElev + lNear + lAdj, data = g, na.action = na.fail)
dm <- dredge(m_all, rank = "AIC", trace = 0)
## Fixed term is "(Intercept)"
d <- as.data.frame(subset(dm, delta < 2, recalc.weights = FALSE))
d <- d[, c("lArea", "lElev", "lNear", "lAdj", "df", "AIC", "delta", "weight")]
d[, 1:4] <- lapply(d[, 1:4], function(v) ifelse(is.na(v), "", sprintf("%.3f", v)))
d$AIC <- round(d$AIC, 1); d$delta <- round(d$delta, 2); d$weight <- round(d$weight, 2)
rownames(d) <- NULL
knitr::kable(d, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2))
lArea lElev lNear lAdj df AIC delta weight
0.376 -0.123 4 273.4 0.00 0.28
0.367 3 274.0 0.61 0.21
0.375 -0.130 -0.030 5 274.7 1.29 0.15
0.371 0.017 -0.125 5 275.4 1.99 0.10

MuMIn::dredge() fits all \(2^4\) = 16 negative-binomial models of Galapagos plant richness (na.action = na.fail makes every model use the same rows). Shown: the models within 2 AIC units of the best.

  • delta = AIC distance to the best model; within 2 units = equivalent
  • weight = each model’s share of the “evidence” (all 16 sum to 1): the best model holds only 29% — there is no single winner
  • lArea is in every competitive model, lNear in most, lElev and lAdj only occasionally and with coefficients near 0 (lElev is collinear with area)

Dredging is criticised as “fishing”: afterwards we act as if we had planned this one model, so its p-values and confidence intervals are wrong (point predictions are fine). Whatever you do — say what you did.

What you will do in practical 5

No code to write — you read and interpret output, as you would in a paper:

  1. Two factors (birdmalariaO): reconstruct the four group means from the coefficients of Sex * mmal; read a sequential ANOVA table; additive or interaction model?
  2. ANCOVA (regrowth): why the boxplot and the coefficient disagree about grazing; two parallel lines from one table; why the order of terms changes the deviance
  3. Continuous × factor interaction (wells, quasi-binomial): two logit equations; non-significant main effects that must stay; F instead of χ²
  4. Negative binomial with interaction (RIKZdat): slopes per exposure class, LR test with 2 df, AIC ranking of four models, back-transforming with exp()
  5. Collinearity (gala): |r| > 0.7, VIF, what happens to elevation once area is in the model
  6. Two continuous predictors (loyn): slopes at grazing 1 and 5, image/contour plot and the empty corners
  7. Model selection (loyn): a step() table, AIC vs BIC results, a dredge() table with delta and weight — and the caveat about the p-values

Take-home messages

  1. A second predictor is one more coefficient — but brings four problems: visualising, interactions, collinearity, model selection.
  2. Visualise with panels or symbols; smooth binary data (LOESS); for two continuous predictors draw the surface (outer → image + contour) with the data points on it.
  3. An interaction = the effect of one predictor depends on the other: non-parallel lines; coded as the product; the coefficient is the change in slope. Main effects then refer to the reference level / x = 0 and must stay in the model (marginality).
  4. Read the fitted equations from the table: reference group = intercept + slope; other groups add their extra intercept and extra slope.
  5. anova() of one model is sequential — order matters when predictors are correlated; anova(m1, m2) compares two nested models.
  6. Collinearity (|r| > 0.7, VIF > 10) makes effects unattributable and estimates unstable: check the predictors before modelling, keep one per group.
  7. Compare candidate models by AIC/BIC (≥ 2 units) or an LR test; simplify backwards (step(), BIC for small n) or search all subsets (dredge(), weights); never forward. Selected models have optimistic p-values — say so.

Dormann, C. F. (2020). Environmental Data Analysis: An Introduction with Examples in R, Chapters 15 and 16. Springer. Data: carData::TitanicSurvival, ISwR::hellung, Paruelo & Lauenroth (1996) via Quinn & Keough (2002), qsbsdata::gala.
